sections.section_title: The River and the Tree of Life
sections.summary: The angel shows John the river of the water of life flowing from the shared throne of God and the Lamb down the center of the city's main street, and the tree of life on both sides of the river bearing twelve kinds of fruit monthly with leaves for the healing of the nations -- fulfilling Ezekiel 47, reversing the barred tree of Genesis 3:24, and completing the promise to the Ephesian overcomer (2:7).

sections.section_title: No More Curse -- The Servants' Eternal Reign
sections.summary: The curse of Genesis 3 is abolished, the throne of God and the Lamb is located within the city, the bond-servants perform unmediated sacred service (latreuō), see God's face (reversing Exodus 33:20), bear his name on their foreheads (fulfilling the priestly consecration of Exodus 28:36-38 and contrasting the beast's mark), and reign forever and ever -- the temporal millennium of 20:4-6 elevated to the eternal.

The angel authenticates the vision as 'faithful and true,' reaffirms the revelation chain of 1:1, and Christ declares 'I am coming quickly,' followed by the sixth beatitude: 'Blessed is he who heeds the words of the prophecy of this book.'
sections.relevance: The sixth beatitude pronounces blessing on 'he who heeds' (ho tērōn) the prophecy, using the same verb tēreō ('to keep, to guard, to observe') as the first beatitude in 1:3. The neutral reading identifies the appropriate response to the document as 'not merely hearing or understanding but keeping -- active, sustained obedience to what has been communicated.' The beatitude implies that blessing is contingent on a genuine human response (keeping the prophecy), not on a predetermined status. However, the passage is not directly arguing about who determines salvation outcomes; it is a conditional blessing that presupposes human agency as the mechanism of response.
key_phrases: Blessed is he who heeds the words of the prophecy of this book

sections.summary: John falls to worship the angel a second time (repeating 19:10), is rebuked with the identification that the angel is a fellow servant (syndoulos) of John, the prophets, and those who keep the book's words, and is commanded: 'Worship God' -- reinforcing the document's central insistence on exclusive divine worship against the backdrop of imperial cult and misdirected reverence.

The angel instructs John not to seal the prophecy (contrasting Daniel 12:4, 9) because the time is near, and four declarations announce that the wrongdoer, the filthy, the righteous, and the holy will each remain in their respective conditions -- signaling the finality of present decisions as the kairos presses upon the assemblies.
sections.relevance: The four aorist imperatives ('let the one who does wrong still do wrong... let the one who is righteous still practice righteousness') declare that the postures people have adopted will define their destiny. The neutral reading interprets these not as divine approval of wrongdoing but as a declaration of 'the finality of the present moment's decisions.' The passage draws on the hardening dynamic of Isaiah 6:9-10, where 'continued rejection results in confirmed rejection,' but the neutral reading frames this as responsive to human choice: 'the revelation has been given, and the response defines the responder.' The trajectories are humanly adopted before being divinely confirmed. Some ambiguity exists because the hardening dynamic could be read as God locking in trajectories, but the dominant emphasis in the neutral reading is that human response to revelation determines the outcome.
key_phrases: Let the one who does wrong, still do wrong
let the one who is righteous, still practice righteousness
the postures people have adopted will define their destiny

sections.section_title: Coming Soon with Reward -- The Alpha and Omega
sections.summary: Christ declares his imminent coming a second time, announces that his reward is with him 'to render to every man according to what he has done' (echoing Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11), and claims the three divine title-pairs -- Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end -- gathering the self-designations distributed between God and the Lamb throughout the document into a single Christological declaration.
sections.relevance: The passage directly addresses how salvation outcomes are determined: 'to render to every man according to what he has done' (apodounai hekastō hōs to ergon estin autou). The criterion is each person's own work (to ergon autou). The neutral reading identifies this as the same principle operative throughout the entire document -- the seven messages ('I know your works'), the great white throne judgment (20:12-13, 'the dead were judged according to their deeds'), and now the returning Christ's own declaration. The reward is individualized (hekastō, 'each one') and deed-based, directly presupposing genuine human agency whose actions constitute the basis of judgment. This is not an aside or illustration but Christ's own direct speech about the criterion governing salvation outcomes, spoken as part of the author's climactic epilogue.
key_phrases: my reward is with me, to render to every man according to what he has done
The overcomer inherits the new creation; the cowardly and faithless receive the second death

sections.section_title: The Seventh Beatitude and the Final Exclusion
sections.summary: The seventh and final beatitude declares blessed those who wash their robes, granting them the right (exousia) to the tree of life and entry through the gates into the city; outside are the dogs, sorcerers, immoral persons, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices lying -- the comprehensive list of those who participated in the beast's system.
sections.relevance: The passage directly connects salvation outcomes to ongoing human behavior. Access to the tree of life and entry into the city are conditional: they belong to 'those who wash their robes' (hoi plynontes tas stolas autōn). The present participle plynontes indicates continuous action -- the neutral reading explicitly states 'not a single past event but a continuous practice' and 'those who persist in the purification that the Lamb's blood provides.' The right (exousia) to the tree is not automatic but belongs to those who meet the condition. Exclusion is equally behavioral: the six categories of the excluded (dogs, sorcerers, immoral, murderers, idolaters, liars) are all defined by their practices, not by a prior divine decree. The neutral reading identifies these as those who participated in the beast's system through their own actions -- 'cultic prostitution, deceptive manipulation, sexual-idolatrous compromise, violence against the faithful, worship of false gods, and alignment with the dragon's deception.' The conditional structure (wash robes → right to tree and city; practice evil → excluded) is the author's climactic beatitude, the seventh in the series, and directly states that human behavior determines access to the new creation.
key_phrases: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life
may enter by the gates into the city
Outside are the dogs and the sorcerers and the immoral persons and the murderers and the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices lying

sections.summary: Jesus identifies himself by name ('I, Jesus'), confirms his role in the revelation chain by declaring he sent his angel to testify to the assemblies, and claims two messianic titles -- 'the root and the descendant of David' (combining preexistence and incarnation via Isaiah 11:1, 10) and 'the bright morning star' (fulfilling Balaam's star prophecy of Numbers 24:17 and identifying himself as what was promised to the Thyatiran overcomer in 2:28).

sections.section_title: The Spirit and the Bride Say 'Come'
sections.summary: The Spirit and the bride jointly cry 'Come' -- directed both toward Christ (calling for his return) and toward the thirsty -- and the invitation extends to every hearer to join the cry; then the passage turns to the open offer: 'let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who wishes take the water of life without cost.'
sections.relevance: This is a conventional proof-text for human agency in salvation, and the neutral reading fully supports that use. The passage directly addresses the availability of salvation (the water of life) and presents it as contingent on two human dispositions: thirst (ho dipsōn, 'the one who thirsts') and willingness (ho thelōn, 'the one who wishes'). The neutral reading explicitly states: 'The only condition is thirst and willingness.' The word dorean ('freely, without cost, as a gift') is contrasted with the beast's coercive economic system (13:17), where access required the beast's mark; in the new creation, 'No mark is required. No allegiance is coerced.' The neutral reading identifies this as 'the document's final evangelistic invitation' and 'the document's final statement on the availability of salvation: it is free, it is offered, and the one who desires it may take it.' The only barrier is 'the hearer's own refusal.' The passage draws on Isaiah 55:1's open invitation, which requires human initiative (coming, buying without money). This is not an aside but the document's climactic invitation, spoken jointly by the Spirit and the bride as part of the author's conclusion, directly addressing who may receive salvation and on what basis.
key_phrases: let the one who is thirsty come
let the one who wishes take the water of life without cost
The only condition is thirst and willingness
The only barrier is the hearer's own refusal

sections.summary: A solemn warning (most likely from the risen Christ) declares that anyone who adds to the prophecy will receive its plagues and anyone who subtracts from it will forfeit their share of the tree of life and the holy city -- applying the Deuteronomic protection formula (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32) to this prophetic document and asserting its completeness and divine authority.
sections.relevance: The passage implies that a human action -- tampering with the prophecy -- can result in loss of one's share (meros) in the tree of life and the holy city. The neutral reading notes that meros ('part, share, portion') appeared in 21:8 for the negative inheritance (lake of fire) and here denotes the positive inheritance that can be forfeited. The logic presupposes that a person possesses a share in the new creation that can be removed as a consequence of their choices. This is not a direct argument about determinism versus agency in salvation broadly, but it does presuppose that human actions affect salvation standing -- one can forfeit what one has by one's own behavior. The passage functions primarily as a textual-integrity warning rather than a soteriological argument, hence the lower confidence.
key_phrases: God will take away his part from the tree of life and from the holy city

sections.section_title: 'Come, Lord Jesus' -- The Final Exchange and Benediction
sections.summary: Christ speaks the third and final 'I am coming quickly,' John (or the liturgical community) responds with 'Amen. Come, Lord Jesus' -- the Greek equivalent of the Aramaic Maranatha preserved in 1 Corinthians 16:22 and the Didache -- and the document closes with an epistolary grace benediction ('The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all') extended universally, completing the epistolary frame opened in 1:4-5.
